description: We are BeatlessFlame, a team passionate about space, robotics, mechanical engineering, physics, and innovation. We aim to explore fire in microgravity and develop creative, science-based solutions. We value teamwork, critical thinking, creativity, and learning. Join us to turn ideas into reality! We welcome members with skills in programming, AI, data analysis, engineering, physics, 3D modeling, scientific research, design, and presentation. All experience levels are welcome!
summary:
FlameGuard is a web app that makes NASA's space-fire research usable by anyone. NASA has burned many materials in microgravity, but the results are buried in long technical reports. FlameGuard turns nine NASA documents (276 PDF pages) into plain answers in English or Turkish: type a cargo item in everyday words, such as "cotton T-shirt" or "headphone cable", and see the closest NASA-tested specimen, what happened when it burned in space, the test conditions, where it flew, and a link to the exact report page.

It answers the Flame in Freefall challenge by summarizing and comparing the evidence without inventing any. Missing data is shown as unknown, never as safe; microgravity results are never reused for the Moon; and every gap becomes a ranked list of tests NASA still needs, starting with a burn test on the lunar surface. An AI assistant gives a short answer plus the verbatim NASA quote as proof, or says the answer is not in the files.

This matters because future Moon and Mars habitats will use oxygen-rich, low-pressure air. Mission planners, students and educators can now check in seconds what used to take hours of reading.
details:
What it does and how it works

FlameGuard turns NASA's space-fire research into answers anyone can use. You choose a place (ISS, lunar habitat, Mars mission or Earth laboratory) and type cargo in everyday words, such as "cotton T-shirt", "headphone cable" or "silicone gasket". FlameGuard matches each item to the closest specimen NASA actually burned in space and shows, in one plain sentence, what happened: how many tests, how often it ignited, whether the flame spread, the oxygen and pressure, and where it flew (ISS, Space Shuttle, Mir or an uncrewed Cygnus vehicle). Every number links to its exact page in the NASA PDF.

If an item comes in several materials (a bottle, a T-shirt), the app asks instead of guessing. If NASA never tested a material (glass, metal, polyester), it says so and never swaps in a different one.

The app has eight pages: Mission Overview, Environment Explorer, Cargo Screening, Material Explorer, Experiment Library, Evidence Gaps, an AI Research Assistant, and Methodology & Sources.

Benefits

- Seconds instead of hours: 9 NASA documents (276 PDF pages) become searchable answers.

- Honest by design: missing data is shown as "unknown", never as "safe"; conflicting numbers are marked "disputed"; results are observed counts with their conditions, not invented probabilities.

- "Same cargo, two worlds": ISS and Moon results side by side. Microgravity data is never reused for lunar gravity.

- A ranked list of "Tests NASA still needs to fly", led by a burn test on the lunar surface.

- A printable PDF mission report and CSV/JSON exports, all from the same evidence and filters.

- Accessible: English and Turkish, read-aloud buttons, a plain-language glossary, text tables for every chart, keyboard and mobile support.

Intended impact

Moon and Mars habitats will use low-pressure, oxygen-rich air, where materials can burn differently. FlameGuard helps mission planners, students and educators find the existing evidence quickly and shows clearly where it is missing, pointing to the experiments that still need to be done.

Tools and technologies

Python 3.12 and Streamlit, pandas, Altair charts, SQLite snapshots with SHA-256 hashes for every source PDF, pypdf for page-level extraction, fpdf2 for the PDF report, NASA 3D models (ISS, Moon, Mars, Earth) rendered with WebGL, the NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) API, optional Google Gemini for quote selection, Playwright for accessibility and mobile testing, GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud. More than 100 automated tests check the data, both languages and every page. We used AI coding assistants to write code and cross-check numbers; the team checked every data row against its PDF page.

How it is creative

Instead of a risk score, which would be a guess, FlameGuard predicts nothing. It starts from everyday words rather than material science terms, turns gaps into a to-do list for future NASA experiments, and its AI assistant answers in plain language while always showing the original NASA quote as proof, or saying "not in the files".

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty (no invented values, no "safe" labels), traceability to the source page, accessibility for non-experts and for people using screen readers, two languages, offline use without paid APIs, and the limits of a small verified dataset, which we state openly. FlameGuard is an independent student project, not NASA-approved and not a flight-safety assessment.
